Σ_{i=1}^{n} i = n(n + 1)/2.title: Sum of the first n integers (arithmetic series)
Σ_{i=1}^{n} i = n(n + 1)/2.about: Adding 1 + 2 + … + n gives n(n + 1)/2. It counts the work of a doubly nested loop where the inner loop runs i times, which is why such loops are Θ(n^{2}).
assumptions: n is a non-negative integer; the empty sum (n = 0) is 0
For a general arithmetic series a, a + d, …, the sum is (number of terms)(first + last)/2
vars: number of terms (the last integer added)

example.problem: A loop compares every pair of 100 items once (inner loop runs i times for i = 1 … 99). How many comparisons?

Σ_{i=0}^{n} 2^{i} = 2^{n+1} − 1.title: Sum of powers of two (geometric series)
Σ_{i=0}^{n} 2^{i} = 2^{n+1} − 1.about: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^{n} is one less than the next power of two. It is why a full binary tree of height n has 2^{n+1} − 1 nodes, and why doubling a dynamic array costs O(1) amortized per insert.
assumptions: n is a non-negative integer
It is the ratio-2 case of the geometric series; for ratio r ≠ 1 use (r^{n+1} − 1)/(r − 1)

example.problem: How many nodes are in a complete binary tree with levels 0 through 9?

T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n).title: Divide-and-conquer recurrence (master theorem form)
T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n).about: A recursive algorithm that splits a problem of size n into a pieces of size n/b and does f(n) extra work satisfies this recurrence. Draw the recursion tree: level i has a^{i} calls each costing f(n/b^{i}), and there are n^{log_{b} a} leaves. The master theorem compares f(n) with n^{log_{b} a}: whichever grows faster sets the total, and if they match every level costs the same, which adds a log n factor.
assumptions: The subproblems are all the same size n/b, with a ≥ 1 and b > 1
The exponent is log_{b} a (log base b of a), not log_{a} b
f(n) is asymptotically positive; floors and ceilings in n/b don’t change the result
There are gaps between the three cases (e.g. f(n) = n^{log_{b} a}/log n); then use a recursion tree or Akra–Bazzi
vars: running time on an input of size n
factor the input shrinks by per call
work done outside the recursive calls (split and combine)
related: case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^{log_{b} a + ε}) and a f(n/b) ≤ c f(n), c < 1

example.problem: Merge sort splits into 2 halves and merges in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Find its order, and estimate the steps for n = 1024.
steps: f(n) = n = Θ(n): case 2, every level costs the same
n = 1024: log_{2} 1024 = 10 levels of about 1024 steps each
example.answer: T(n) = Θ(n log n); about 10,240 steps for n = 1024

T(n) = Θ(n^{log_{b} a}).title: Master theorem case 1: the leaves dominate
T(n) = Θ(n^{log_{b} a}).about: When the work outside the recursion, f(n), grows polynomially slower than n^{log_{b} a}, the cost of the a^{log_{b} n} = n^{log_{b} a} leaves dominates and sets the running time.
assumptions: Needs f(n) = O(n^{log_{b} a − ε}) for some ε > 0, polynomially smaller, not just smaller by a log factor
The subproblems are all the same size n/b, with a ≥ 1 and b > 1
vars: running time on an input of size n
factor the input shrinks by per call
work done outside the recursive calls (split and combine)
related: case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^{log_{b} a + ε}) and a f(n/b) ≤ c f(n), c < 1

example.problem: Karatsuba multiplication makes 3 recursive multiplications of half-size numbers plus linear work: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n. Find its order.
steps: f(n) = n = O(n^{1.585 − ε}) with ε ≈ 0.5: case 1

T(n) = Θ(n^{log_{b} a} log n).title: Master theorem case 2: every level costs the same
T(n) = Θ(n^{log_{b} a} log n).about: When f(n) matches n^{log_{b} a}, each of the log_{b} n levels of the recursion tree does about the same work, so the total is that work times the number of levels.
assumptions: Needs f(n) = Θ(n^{log_{b} a}) exactly; if f(n) = Θ(n^{log_{b} a} log^{k} n) the answer becomes Θ(n^{log_{b} a} log^{k+1} n)
The subproblems are all the same size n/b, with a ≥ 1 and b > 1
vars: running time on an input of size n
factor the input shrinks by per call
work done outside the recursive calls (split and combine)
related: case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^{log_{b} a + ε}) and a f(n/b) ≤ c f(n), c < 1

example.problem: A divide-and-conquer matrix routine makes 4 half-size calls and does n^{2} extra work: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^{2}. Find its order, and estimate the work for n = 1024.
steps: f(n) = n^{2} = Θ(n^{2}): case 2, each of the log_{2} n levels costs about n^{2}
example.answer: Θ(n^{2} log n); about 1.05 × 10^{7} steps for n = 1024

T(n) = Θ(f(n)).title: Master theorem case 3: the root's work dominates
T(n) = Θ(f(n)).about: When f(n) grows polynomially faster than n^{log_{b} a}, the top-level split and combine cost more than everything below, and the running time is just f(n).
assumptions: Needs f(n) = Ω(n^{log_{b} a + ε}) for some ε > 0
And the regularity condition a f(n/b) ≤ c f(n) for some c < 1 and large n, so the work shrinks geometrically down the tree (it holds for ordinary polynomials)
The subproblems are all the same size n/b, with a ≥ 1 and b > 1
vars: running time on an input of size n
factor the input shrinks by per call
work done outside the recursive calls (split and combine)
related: case 3: f(n) = Ω(n^{log_{b} a + ε}) and a f(n/b) ≤ c f(n), c < 1

example.problem: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^{2}, and add up the levels for n = 1024.
steps: Level i costs n^{2}/2^{i}: a geometric series, so the total stays under 2n^{2} and the root’s n^{2} dominates
example.answer: T(n) = Θ(n^{2}); for n = 1024 the levels add to 2,096,128 ≈ 2n^{2}

α = n/m.title: Hash table load factor
α = n/m.about: The load factor is the average number of keys per bucket. It sets the expected cost of a lookup, so tables resize (typically doubling m) once α passes a threshold.
assumptions: Assumes simple uniform hashing: each key is equally likely to land in any bucket, independently
Chaining tolerates α > 1; open addressing needs α < 1 and slows sharply as α → 1
related: expected probes for an unsuccessful search, open addressing

example.problem: A hash table with open addressing has 1024 slots holding 750 keys. Find α and the expected probes for an unsuccessful search.

P ≈ 1 − e^{−n^{2}/(2m)}.title: Birthday bound: chance of a hash collision
P ≈ 1 − e^{−n^{2}/(2m)}.about: With n items hashed into m equally likely values, the probability that at least two share a value is about 1 − e^{−n^{2}/(2m)}. Collisions become likely once n is near √m, far sooner than intuition suggests.
assumptions: Hash values are uniform and independent
An approximation good for n ≪ m; the exact value is 1 − Π_{k=0}^{n−1}(1 − k/m)
Some texts use n(n − 1) in place of n^{2}; the difference is small for large n
vars: probability of at least one collision

example.problem: How likely is a collision among 23 people's birthdays (m = 365)?

N = 2^{n}.title: Number of values in n bits
N = 2^{n}.about: Each bit doubles the number of distinct patterns, so n bits can represent 2^{n} different values: unsigned integers 0 to 2^{n} − 1, or −2^{n−1} to 2^{n−1} − 1 in two's complement.
assumptions: Counts distinct bit patterns; how they map to values (unsigned, signed, floating point) is a separate choice

example.problem: How many distinct addresses does a 32-bit IPv4 address allow?

n = log_{2}(N).title: Bits needed to encode N values
n = log_{2}(N).about: To give each of N things its own binary code you need log_{2}(N) bits, rounded up to a whole bit. It is also the number of yes/no questions binary search needs to find one item among N.
assumptions: Round up: n = ⌈log_{2} N⌉ for a fixed-width code
Assumes every value gets a code of the same length; variable-length codes average down to the entropy H
vars: number of distinct values to represent

example.problem: How many bits are needed to give each of 1000 sensors a unique ID?

H = −Σ p_{i} log_{2}(p_{i}).title: Shannon entropy
H = −Σ p_{i} log_{2}(p_{i}).about: Entropy is the average information per symbol from a source, in bits. It is the lower bound on the average code length of any lossless compression of that source.
assumptions: The p_{i} are probabilities that sum to 1; a term with p_{i} = 0 counts as 0
Symbols are independent draws; correlated sources (like English text) have a lower entropy rate
With ln instead of log_{2} the unit is nats
related: average length of any lossless code

example.problem: A source emits A, B, C with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.25. Find its entropy.

S = 1/((1 − p) + p/s).title: Amdahl's law: overall speedup
S = 1/((1 − p) + p/s).about: Speeding up only part of a program by a factor s speeds up the whole by S. The untouched fraction 1 − p caps the speedup at 1/(1 − p) no matter how large s gets.
assumptions: The fraction p is measured as a share of the original run time
The workload size is fixed (strong scaling); if the problem grows with the processors, Gustafson's law applies
Ignores the overhead of communication and synchronization, which lowers S in practice
vars: fraction of the original time that is sped up
speedup of that fraction (e.g. number of cores)

example.problem: 90% of a program parallelizes perfectly. What is the speedup on 8 cores?

t = N CPI/f.title: CPU time (the iron law of performance)
t = N CPI/f.about: Run time is instructions executed × average clock cycles per instruction ÷ clock frequency. It shows the three levers: fewer instructions, fewer cycles each, or a faster clock.
assumptions: CPI is an average over the actual instruction mix and includes stalls (cache misses, branch mispredictions)
Ignores time waiting on I/O or other processes

example.problem: A program runs 2 × 10^{9} instructions at a CPI of 1.5 on a 3 GHz processor. How long does it take?

AMAT = t_{hit} + m t_{miss}.title: Average memory access time
AMAT = t_{hit} + m t_{miss}.about: Every access pays the cache hit time; the fraction that miss also pay the miss penalty. It is how cache size, associativity and multi-level caches are compared.
assumptions: m is the miss rate per access at this level (0 to 1)
t_{miss} is the extra time to fetch from the next level; for multi-level caches it is itself an AMAT
Ignores overlap of misses (out-of-order or non-blocking caches hide part of the penalty)

example.problem: An L1 cache hits in 1 ns, misses 5% of the time, and a miss costs 100 ns. Find the AMAT.

t = L/R.title: Transmission delay
t = L/R.about: The time to push all of a packet's bits onto the link: its length divided by the link's bit rate. It depends on the packet and the link speed, not on distance.
assumptions: R is the link's data rate (bits per second), not the signal's propagation speed
Watch units: packet sizes are often in bytes (× 8 bits) and rates use powers of 10 (1 Mb/s = 10^{6} b/s)

example.problem: How long does it take to transmit a 1500-byte packet on a 100 Mb/s link?

t = d/s.title: Propagation delay
t = d/s.about: The time for a signal to travel the length of a link: distance over propagation speed. It is independent of the packet size and the bit rate.
assumptions: s is the signal speed in the medium: about 2 × 10^{8} m/s in copper or fibre (≈ 2/3 c), 3 × 10^{8} m/s in air or vacuum

example.problem: Light in fibre travels at 2 × 10^{8} m/s. What is the one-way propagation delay over 4000 km of fibre?

BDP = R RTT.title: Bandwidth-delay product
BDP = R RTT.about: The amount of data in flight on a link: the rate times the round-trip time. A sender's window (TCP window, buffer) must be at least this big to keep the link fully used.
assumptions: Uses the round-trip time, since the sender waits a full RTT for acknowledgements; some texts use the one-way delay for 'bits on the wire'
R is the bottleneck rate along the path

example.problem: A 1 Gb/s path has a 50 ms round-trip time. How large a window keeps it full?

ŷ = w · x + b.title: Linear model
ŷ = w · x + b.about: A linear model predicts a weighted sum of the input features plus a bias. It is linear regression when ŷ is used directly, and the score inside logistic regression and every neuron of a network.
assumptions: The output is linear in each feature; curved relations need engineered features (x^{2}, log x) or a nonlinear model
For least squares, errors should be independent with constant variance for the usual confidence intervals
vars: weight vector, one weight per feature

example.problem: A house-price model has w = (150, 10,000) for (area in m^{2}, bedrooms) and b = 20,000. Predict the price of a 120 m^{2}, 3-bedroom house.

w = (X^{T} X)^{−1} X^{T} y.title: Normal equation: least-squares weights
w = (X^{T} X)^{−1} X^{T} y.about: The weights that minimise the squared error of a linear model, found in one step from the data matrix X and targets y, without gradient descent. Setting the gradient of ‖Xw − y‖^{2} to zero gives X^{T}X w = X^{T}y: the leftover error must be perpendicular to every feature column. In code, solve that system rather than forming the inverse.
assumptions: X^{T} X must be invertible: more examples than features and no feature an exact combination of others; otherwise use the pseudo-inverse or ridge regression
Add a column of ones to X to fit the bias
Costs O(d^{3}) in the number of features d, so gradient descent wins for very many features
vars: data matrix, one row per example (n × d)

σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^{−z}).title: Sigmoid (logistic) function
σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^{−z}).about: The sigmoid squashes any real number into (0, 1), so it turns a linear score into a probability in logistic regression and binary classifiers. It is the inverse of the log-odds: z = ln(p/(1 − p)), so z = 0 means even odds (σ = 1/2) and each +1 in z multiplies the odds by e.
assumptions: Saturates for large |z|: its gradient σ(1 − σ) vanishes, which slows training of deep networks (ReLU avoids this)
For large negative z compute it as e^{z}/(1 + e^{z}) to avoid overflow

example.problem: A logistic regression scores an email z = 2. What probability of spam does it give?

p_{i} = e^{z_{i}}/(Σ_{j} e^{z_{j}}).title: Softmax
p_{i} = e^{z_{i}}/(Σ_{j} e^{z_{j}}).about: Softmax turns a vector of scores (logits) into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1, with the largest score getting the largest share. It is the output layer of multi-class classifiers.
assumptions: Subtracting max(z) from every z_{i} first gives the same result and avoids overflow
Only differences between scores matter: adding a constant to all z_{i} changes nothing
With two classes it reduces to the sigmoid of z_{1} − z_{2}
related: cross-entropy loss with a one-hot label

example.problem: A classifier gives scores (2, 1, 0.1) for three classes. Find the probability of the first class.

ReLU(z) = max(0, z).title: ReLU (rectified linear unit)
ReLU(z) = max(0, z).about: ReLU passes positive inputs unchanged and zeroes negative ones. Stacking layers of it gives a network made of many flat pieces that can bend to fit any shape. It is the default activation in deep networks because it is cheap and its gradient is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so it doesn’t vanish the way the sigmoid’s does.
assumptions: Not differentiable at 0; the gradient there is taken as 0 (or 1)
A unit whose input stays negative gets zero gradient and stops learning ('dying ReLU'); Leaky ReLU max(αz, z) keeps a small slope
related: Leaky ReLU, small α such as 0.01

example.problem: A neuron has weights (0.4, −0.2) and bias 0.1. What does it output for the inputs (3, 1) and (1, 4)?

MSE = (1/n) Σ (y_{i} − ŷ_{i})^{2}.title: Mean squared error
MSE = (1/n) Σ (y_{i} − ŷ_{i})^{2}.about: The average of the squared differences between targets and predictions: the standard loss for regression. Squaring makes every error count positive and punishes large errors heavily; a model trained on it predicts the mean of y. Judge it on held-out data: a low training MSE with a high validation MSE means overfitting.
assumptions: Sensitive to outliers; mean absolute error is more robust
Its units are the target's units squared; RMSE = √MSE is back in the target's units
Minimising it is maximum likelihood when the errors are Gaussian with constant variance

example.problem: Targets (3, 5, 2) are predicted as (2.5, 5, 4). Find the MSE.

L = −Σ y_{i} ln(ŷ_{i}).title: Cross-entropy loss
L = −Σ y_{i} ln(ŷ_{i}).about: The loss for classification: minus the log of the probability the model gave the true class. Confident wrong answers are punished heavily; a perfect prediction costs 0.
assumptions: y is a probability distribution over classes, usually one-hot (1 for the true class), so only that class's term survives
ŷ_{i} must be > 0; clip it or compute from logits to avoid ln(0)
Averaged over a batch in practice
vars: true probability of class i (1 for the true class)
related: L = −(y ln ŷ + (1 − y) ln(1 − ŷ))

example.problem: A classifier gives the true class probability 0.7. What is the loss? And at 0.1?

D = Σ p_{i} ln(p_{i}/q_{i}).title: Kullback–Leibler divergence
D = Σ p_{i} ln(p_{i}/q_{i}).about: KL divergence measures how much a distribution q differs from a reference p: the extra information needed when q is used to code data from p. It is zero only when the two are equal.
assumptions: Not symmetric: D(p ‖ q) ≠ D(q ‖ p), so it is not a distance
Infinite if some q_{i} = 0 where p_{i} > 0; terms with p_{i} = 0 count as 0
In nats with ln; use log_{2} for bits
vars: KL divergence of q from p

example.problem: A fair coin p = (0.5, 0.5) is modelled as q = (0.9, 0.1). Find D(p ‖ q).

L + λ ‖w‖^{2}.title: L2 regularization (weight decay, ridge)
L + λ ‖w‖^{2}.about: Adding λ times the squared length of the weight vector to the loss pulls the weights toward zero. Large weights let a model bend to fit the noise in its training data; penalising them trades a little training error for a smoother model that does better on new data (less overfitting).
assumptions: The bias is usually left out of ‖w‖^{2}
Features should be on similar scales, since the penalty treats every weight alike
Choose λ by validation; too large underfits
vars: sum of squared weights Σ w_{j}^{2}
related: gradient step: weights decay each step

example.problem: A model has loss 0.8 and weights (2, −1, 0.5). With λ = 0.01, what is the regularized loss?

w ← w − η ∇L.title: Gradient descent update
w ← w − η ∇L.about: The gradient points uphill, so a small step against it lowers the loss fastest. Repeated, it walks downhill to a minimum; the learning rate η sets the step size.
assumptions: η too large overshoots and diverges; too small crawls
Finds a local minimum; only a convex loss guarantees the global one
Scale the features first, or the loss surface is a long narrow valley and the steps zigzag
Stochastic gradient descent uses the gradient on a mini-batch, a noisy but cheap estimate
vars: gradient of the loss with respect to w
related: stability for a quadratic with largest curvature L_{max}

example.problem: Minimise L(w) = (w − 3)^{2} from w = 0 with η = 0.1. Where is w after one step and after two?

P = TP/(TP + FP).title: Precision
P = TP/(TP + FP).about: Of everything the model flagged positive, the fraction that really is: ‘when it says yes, how often is it right?’. High precision means few false alarms, which matters when acting on a false alarm is costly.
assumptions: Undefined when the model flags nothing (TP + FP = 0)
Don’t mix it up with recall: precision divides by what was flagged, recall by what really is positive
Trades off against recall: raising the decision threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall

example.problem: A spam filter flags 50 emails; 45 are spam. Find its precision.

R = TP/(TP + FN).title: Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate)
R = TP/(TP + FN).about: Of all the real positives, the fraction the model caught: ‘of what it should find, how much did it find?’. High recall means few misses, which matters for screening, fraud and safety faults, where a miss is costly.
assumptions: Undefined if there are no real positives
Trades off against precision; flagging everything gives recall 1

example.problem: There are 60 spam emails; the filter catches 45 of them. Find its recall.

F_{1} = 2PR/(P + R).title: F1 score
F_{1} = 2PR/(P + R).about: The harmonic mean of precision and recall: a single score that is high only when both are. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so P = 1 with R = 0.1 scores 0.18, where the plain average would say 0.55. Preferred over accuracy for imbalanced classes.
assumptions: Weights precision and recall equally; F_{β} weights recall β times as much
Ignores true negatives

example.problem: A filter has precision 0.9 and recall 0.75. Find F1.

A = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN).title: Accuracy
A = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN).about: The fraction of all predictions that are correct. Simple, but misleading when one class is rare: always compare it with the baseline of predicting the commonest class.
assumptions: With imbalanced classes a trivial model scores high: always predicting ‘not fraud’ is 99% accurate if 1% is fraud. Use precision, recall or F1 there
Measure it on held-out data; training accuracy flatters an overfit model

example.problem: Of 1000 emails, a filter gets TP = 45, TN = 930, FP = 5, FN = 20. Find its accuracy.

cos(θ) = (a · b)/(|a| |b|).title: Angle between vectors (cosine similarity)
cos(θ) = (a · b)/(|a| |b|).about: The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 when they point the same way, 0 when perpendicular, −1 when opposite. Take acos of it for the angle itself (between two forces or members); in machine learning the same number, called cosine similarity, compares text embeddings regardless of their length.
assumptions: Neither vector may be zero
Ignores magnitude: (1, 1) and (5, 5) have similarity 1
For non-negative vectors (word counts) it lies between 0 and 1

example.problem: Find the cosine similarity of a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (2, 1, 0).

T^{2} = 4π^{2} a^{3}/(G M).title: Kepler's third law
T^{2} = 4π^{2} a^{3}/(G M).about: The square of an orbit's period is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis. Given one, it finds the other, or weighs the central body from an orbiting moon or planet.
assumptions: The orbiting body's mass m is small next to M; otherwise use G(M + m)
Only the two bodies interact (no perturbations), Newtonian gravity
a is the semi-major axis, measured from the centre of the central body, not from its surface
related: around the Sun, with T in years and a in AU

example.problem: A GPS satellite orbits with a = 26,560 km around the Earth (M = 5.972 × 10^{24} kg). Find its period.

v = √(G M/r).title: Circular orbital speed
v = √(G M/r).about: The speed at which gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force for a circular orbit of radius r. Lower orbits are faster.
assumptions: A circular orbit; for an ellipse use vis-viva
The orbiting mass is small next to M
r is measured from the centre of the central body
vars: orbit radius from the body's centre
related: escape speed at the same r

example.problem: The ISS orbits about 420 km above the Earth (radius 6371 km, M = 5.972 × 10^{24} kg). How fast does it go?

v_{e} = √(2 G M/r).title: Escape velocity
v_{e} = √(2 G M/r).about: The launch speed at which kinetic energy just equals the gravitational potential energy needed to coast to infinity. It does not depend on the direction or on the escaping mass.
assumptions: No air drag and no thrust after launch
Measured relative to the body, ignoring its rotation and other bodies
r is from the body's centre (the surface radius for a launch from the ground)

example.problem: Find the escape speed from the Earth's surface (M = 5.972 × 10^{24} kg, R = 6371 km).

v^{2} = G M (2/r − 1/a).title: Vis-viva equation
v^{2} = G M (2/r − 1/a).about: Gives an orbiting body's speed at any distance r on an ellipse with semi-major axis a. It is energy conservation for a Kepler orbit and the workhorse of transfer-orbit (Hohmann) calculations.
assumptions: Two-body Newtonian motion with the orbiting mass small next to M
a > 0 for an ellipse; a → ∞ gives escape speed; a < 0 for a hyperbola
r and a measured from the central body's centre
vars: current distance from the body's centre

example.problem: A Hohmann transfer from 6,671 km to 42,164 km (geostationary) radius has a = 24,418 km. Find the speed at perigee (Earth GM = 3.986 × 10^{14} m^{3}/s^{2}).

g = G M/r^{2}.title: Gravitational acceleration (surface gravity)
g = G M/r^{2}.about: Newton's law of gravitation gives the acceleration a mass M produces at distance r. At a planet's surface r is its radius; higher up, g falls with the square of the distance from the centre.
assumptions: The body is spherically symmetric (then it acts as a point mass at its centre)
Outside the body; inside a uniform sphere g grows linearly with r
Ignores rotation, which lowers apparent g at the equator by about 0.3%

example.problem: Find the surface gravity of Mars (M = 6.417 × 10^{23} kg, R = 3390 km).

r_{s} = 2 G M/c^{2}.title: Schwarzschild radius
r_{s} = 2 G M/c^{2}.about: The radius of the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole of mass M: compressed inside it, not even light escapes. It is where the Newtonian escape speed would equal c.
assumptions: A non-rotating, uncharged mass (Schwarzschild solution); a spinning (Kerr) hole's horizon is smaller
General relativity; the Newtonian derivation happens to give the same formula

example.problem: Find the Schwarzschild radius of the Sun (M = 1.989 × 10^{30} kg).

L = 4π R^{2} σ T^{4}.title: Stefan–Boltzmann law: a star's luminosity
L = 4π R^{2} σ T^{4}.about: A star's total power output is its surface area times σT^{4}, the flux from each square metre of a black body. Doubling the temperature multiplies the luminosity by 16; with L and T known, it gives the star's radius, which is how giants are recognized.
assumptions: The star radiates as a black body; T is the effective (surface) temperature in kelvin
Spherical star of radius R (radius, not diameter)

example.problem: Find the Sun's luminosity (R = 6.96 × 10^{8} m, T = 5772 K).

λ_{max} = b/T.title: Wien's displacement law
λ_{max} = b/T.about: A black body's spectrum peaks at a wavelength inversely proportional to its temperature: hot stars look blue, cool stars red. From a star's colour it gives the surface temperature.
assumptions: Black-body emission
This is the peak per unit wavelength; per unit frequency the peak sits elsewhere

example.problem: The Sun's surface is at 5772 K. Where does its spectrum peak?

F = L/(4π d^{2}).title: Flux: the inverse-square law
F = L/(4π d^{2}).about: Light spreads over a sphere of area 4πd^{2}, so the power per unit area received falls with the square of the distance. With measured flux and known luminosity it gives the distance (a standard candle).
assumptions: The source radiates equally in all directions
No absorption by dust or gas on the way (extinction)
Distances short enough to ignore cosmological redshift
vars: flux (power per unit area) at the observer

example.problem: The Sun (L = 3.828 × 10^{26} W) is 1.496 × 10^{11} m from the Earth. What flux reaches the Earth?

m − M = 5 log_{10}(d) − 5.title: Distance modulus
m − M = 5 log_{10}(d) − 5.about: The difference between how bright a star looks (apparent magnitude m) and how bright it would look from 10 parsecs (absolute magnitude M) gives its distance. Each 5 magnitudes is a factor of 10 in distance.
assumptions: d is in parsecs
Ignores extinction; with dust add A: m − M = 5 log_{10} d − 5 + A
Magnitudes run backwards: larger is fainter

example.problem: A Cepheid has absolute magnitude M = −4 and appears at m = 11. How far away is it?

d = 1/p.title: Parallax distance
d = 1/p.about: As the Earth orbits, a nearby star shifts against distant ones. Half that annual shift, the parallax angle p in arcseconds, gives the distance in parsecs directly; this is the definition of the parsec.
assumptions: p in arcseconds gives d in parsecs
Small angles; reliable out to a few thousand parsecs with Gaia
p in arcseconds, not milliarcseconds (divide mas by 1000 first)

example.problem: Proxima Centauri has a parallax of 0.768 arcsec. How far is it, in parsecs and light-years?

v = H_{0} d.title: Hubble's law
v = H_{0} d.about: Distant galaxies recede at a speed proportional to their distance, the signature of an expanding universe. Measuring a galaxy's redshift (and so v) gives its distance.
assumptions: H_{0} ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc (measurements range 67–73)
Valid for galaxies far enough that their own motions (a few hundred km/s) are small, and near enough that v ≪ c
Beyond z ≈ 0.1 the expansion history matters

example.problem: A galaxy recedes at 7000 km/s. With H_{0} = 70 km/s/Mpc, how far away is it?

z = Δλ/λ.title: Redshift
z = Δλ/λ.about: The fractional stretch of a spectral line's wavelength. Positive z means the source is moving away (or space has expanded); for small z the speed is about cz.
assumptions: λ is the rest (laboratory) wavelength and Δλ = λ_{obs} − λ_{rest}
v ≈ cz only for z ≪ 1; for larger z use relativistic or cosmological relations
Negative z is a blueshift (approaching)

example.problem: The hydrogen-alpha line (656.3 nm at rest) is seen at 662.9 nm. Find z and the speed.

A = P(1 + r t).title: Simple interest
A = P(1 + r t).about: Simple interest is paid only on the original principal, never on past interest, so the balance grows by the same P r every period: a straight line, not a curve. Used for short-term loans, bonds’ accrued interest and some car loans.
assumptions: r and t in the same time unit: 6% a year for 18 months is t = 1.5, not 18
Interest is not reinvested

example.problem: $5,000 is lent at 6% simple interest for 3 years. How much is repaid?

A = P(1 + r/n)^{n t}.title: Compound interest
A = P(1 + r/n)^{n t}.about: Each compounding period multiplies the balance by (1 + r/n), and there are n t periods, so interest earns interest and the balance grows exponentially. More frequent compounding helps only a little, approaching P e^{rt}.
assumptions: r is the nominal annual rate; r/n is the rate per period (6% compounded monthly is 0.5% a month, not 6%)
The exponent counts periods, n t, not years
Constant rate, with no deposits or withdrawals in between (add an annuity for those)

example.problem: $10,000 at 5% compounded monthly for 10 years grows to how much?

A = P e^{r t}.title: Continuous compounding
A = P e^{r t}.about: The limit of compounding infinitely often: (1 + r/n)^{n t} → e^{rt} as n → ∞. It is the natural model for exponential growth and decay, and the form used in derivative pricing.
assumptions: r is the continuously compounded annual rate, constant
Only slightly more than daily compounding in practice

example.problem: $10,000 grows at 5% continuously compounded for 10 years. Find the amount.

t ≈ 72/r.title: Rule of 72: doubling time
t ≈ 72/r.about: Dividing 72 by the annual growth rate in percent estimates how many years it takes to double. A quick mental check on any compound growth.
assumptions: r is in percent per period (8 for 8%), and t comes out in the same periods
Most accurate for rates around 6–10%; for continuous growth 69.3/r is exact
Assumes constant compounded growth

example.problem: How long does money take to double at 8% a year? Compare with the exact time.

PV = FV/(1 + r)^{n}.title: Present value
PV = FV/(1 + r)^{n}.about: A sum received n periods from now is worth less today, because today’s money could be invested at rate r. Discounting is FV = PV(1 + r)^{n} run backwards: it brings future cash back to today’s value.
assumptions: r is the discount rate per period and n the number of periods: monthly periods at 6% a year are r = 0.005, n = 12 × years
A single lump sum; a stream of payments needs NPV or the annuity formulas

example.problem: What is $10,000 received in 5 years worth today at a 6% discount rate?

NPV = Σ C_{t}/(1 + r)^{t}.title: Net present value
NPV = Σ C_{t}/(1 + r)^{t}.about: The sum of all cash flows, each discounted back to today. Discounting at r compares the project with simply investing the money at r, so a positive NPV means the project earns more than r and adds value.
assumptions: C_{0} is usually the (negative) initial investment at t = 0 and is not discounted; spreadsheet NPV() starts at t = 1, so add C_{0} separately
Cash flows at the end of each period, with a constant discount rate
The rate at which NPV = 0 is the internal rate of return (IRR)
vars: net cash flow at period t

example.problem: A project costs $1,000 now and returns $400 a year for 3 years. At 8%, is it worth it?

CAGR = (V_{f}/V_{i})^{1/n} − 1.title: Compound annual growth rate
CAGR = (V_{f}/V_{i})^{1/n} − 1.about: The constant yearly rate that would take a value from its start to its end over n years. It smooths a bumpy history into one comparable number.
assumptions: Uses only the start and end values; says nothing about volatility in between
Ignores deposits and withdrawals along the way
n is the number of years (periods) between the two values

example.problem: An investment grew from $10,000 to $18,000 over 5 years. Find the CAGR.

FV = PMT ((1 + r)^{n} − 1)/r.title: Future value of an annuity
FV = PMT ((1 + r)^{n} − 1)/r.about: What a series of equal payments, each earning compound interest, grows to after n periods. Used for savings plans and retirement contributions.
assumptions: Payments at the end of each period (ordinary annuity); for payments at the start multiply by (1 + r)
r is the rate per payment period (annual rate/12 for monthly payments) and n the number of payments
r ≠ 0; with r = 0, FV = n PMT

example.problem: You save $200 a month for 30 years at 6% a year compounded monthly. How much do you have?

PV = PMT (1 − (1 + r)^{−n})/r.title: Present value of an annuity
PV = PMT (1 − (1 + r)^{−n})/r.about: What a series of equal future payments is worth today. It prices a pension, a lottery paid in instalments, or the loan a given payment can support.
assumptions: Payments at the end of each period; for payments at the start multiply by (1 + r)
r is the rate per payment period and n the number of payments
As n → ∞ it tends to PMT/r (a perpetuity)
related: the same equation solved for the payment

example.problem: What are 20 yearly payments of $5,000 worth today at 7%?

M = P r/(1 − (1 + r)^{−n}).title: Loan (mortgage) payment
M = P r/(1 − (1 + r)^{−n}).about: The fixed payment that pays off a loan of P, interest included, in n equal instalments. Early payments are mostly interest; later ones mostly principal.
assumptions: Fixed rate, with r the rate per payment period (annual rate/12 for monthly)
Payments at the end of each period
Excludes taxes, insurance and fees

example.problem: A $300,000 mortgage at 6% a year over 30 years, paid monthly. Find the payment.

ROI = gain/cost.title: Return on investment
ROI = gain/cost.about: Net gain divided by what you put in, usually given as a percentage. A quick way to compare investments.
assumptions: 'gain' here is the net profit (final value − cost); some write (final − cost)/cost explicitly
Ignores how long it took; annualize with CAGR to compare investments of different lengths
Ignores risk

example.problem: A $2,000 marketing campaign brings in $2,600 of extra profit. Find the ROI.

Q = F/(p − v).title: Break-even quantity
Q = F/(p − v).about: The number of units to sell before profit turns positive: fixed costs divided by the contribution margin, what each unit adds after its own variable cost.
assumptions: Constant price and variable cost per unit, whatever the volume
Fixed costs stay fixed over the range considered
p > v; otherwise you never break even

example.problem: A café has $6,000 a month in fixed costs and sells coffee for $4.50 that costs $1.50 to make. How many cups to break even?

r_{real} = (1 + r)/(1 + i) − 1.title: Real interest rate (Fisher equation)
r_{real} = (1 + r)/(1 + i) − 1.about: The growth in purchasing power after inflation. A 5% return in a year of 3% inflation leaves you only about 1.94% richer in goods.
assumptions: r and i are rates over the same period, as decimals
The approximation r_{real} ≈ r − i is fine when both are small
Uses the realized (or expected) inflation rate; taxes are ignored

example.problem: A savings account pays 5% while inflation is 3%. What is the real return?

F(s) = ∫_{0}^{∞} f(t) e^{−st} dt.title: Laplace transform (one-sided definition)
F(s) = ∫_{0}^{∞} f(t) e^{−st} dt.about: The Laplace transform turns a function of time into a function of complex frequency s. Derivatives become multiplication by s, so linear differential equations with initial conditions become algebra.
assumptions: The integral converges only for Re(s) greater than some σ_{0} (the region of convergence); f must grow no faster than an exponential e^{σ_{0}t}
f is piecewise continuous; the lower limit is taken as 0⁻ so an impulse at t = 0 is included
One-sided: it ignores f for t < 0, and brings initial conditions in through the derivative rule
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0
related: inverse transform (in practice: partial fractions and a table)
Fourier transform, when the region includes the jω axis

example.problem: Find the Laplace transform of e^{−2t} from the definition, and evaluate it at s = 3.

u(t) ‖ 1/s.title: Laplace pair: unit step
u(t) ‖ 1/s.about: The unit step switches on at t = 0 and stays at 1; its transform is 1/s, a pole at the origin. Any constant input c (a battery switched on, a constant force) becomes c/s.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > 0
vars: unit step: 0 for t < 0, 1 for t ≥ 0
related: invert by partial fractions, then read each term off this table

example.problem: Solve y′ + 2y = u(t) with y(0) = 0, and find y at t = 1 s.

t ‖ 1/s^{2}.title: Laplace pair: unit ramp
t ‖ 1/s^{2}.about: A ramp rising at slope 1 transforms to 1/s^{2}, a double pole at the origin. It is the input for steady-state tracking error (velocity error constant) in control.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > 0
related: invert by partial fractions, then read each term off this table

example.problem: Solve y′ + y = t with y(0) = 0, and find y(2).

t^{n} ‖ n!/s^{n+1}.title: Laplace pair: power of t
t^{n} ‖ n!/s^{n+1}.about: Each power of t adds one more pole at the origin. Read backwards, it inverts any term c/s^{k}.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
n is a non-negative integer (for real n use Γ(n + 1)/s^{n+1})
Region of convergence Re(s) > 0

example.problem: Find the inverse transform of 12/s^{5} and evaluate it at t = 2.

e^{−at} ‖ 1/(s + a).title: Laplace pair: decaying exponential
e^{−at} ‖ 1/(s + a).about: A single real pole at s = −a is an exponential with time constant 1/a. Most partial-fraction terms invert with this pair.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > −a
a may be negative (a growing exponential, unstable pole in the right half plane) or complex
related: invert by partial fractions, then read each term off this table

example.problem: Find y(t) for Y(s) = 5/((s + 1)(s + 3)), and its value at t = 1.

t e^{−at} ‖ 1/(s + a)^{2}.title: Laplace pair: repeated real pole
t e^{−at} ‖ 1/(s + a)^{2}.about: A double pole at s = −a gives t e^{−at}, which rises then decays. It is the critically damped response.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > −a

example.problem: A critically damped system y″ + 4y′ + 4y = 0 starts with y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 1. Find y(t) and its peak.
example.answer: y = t e^{−2t}; peak 0.184 at t = 0.5

t^{n} e^{−at} ‖ n!/(s + a)^{n+1}.title: Laplace pair: pole of order n + 1
t^{n} e^{−at} ‖ n!/(s + a)^{n+1}.about: The general repeated real pole. Combining the power rule with the frequency shift, it inverts any term c/(s + a)^{k} in a partial-fraction expansion.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
n a non-negative integer
Region of convergence Re(s) > −a
vars: one less than the pole's order
related: frequency shift, the rule behind it

example.problem: Invert F(s) = 2/(s + 1)^{3} and find f(2).
steps: n + 1 = 3 so n = 2, and n! = 2 matches the numerator

sin(ωt) ‖ ω/(s^{2} + ω^{2}).title: Laplace pair: sine
sin(ωt) ‖ ω/(s^{2} + ω^{2}).about: A pair of poles on the imaginary axis at ±jω is an undamped oscillation. The ω in the numerator marks a sine; a numerator s marks a cosine.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > 0
ω in rad/s; the argument ωt is in radians

example.problem: Invert Y(s) = 10/(s^{2} + 25) and evaluate at t = 0.3 s.

cos(ωt) ‖ s/(s^{2} + ω^{2}).title: Laplace pair: cosine
cos(ωt) ‖ s/(s^{2} + ω^{2}).about: The cosine has the same poles ±jω as the sine but a zero at the origin. It appears when an oscillator starts from a displacement rather than a push.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > 0
ω in rad/s; ωt in radians

example.problem: A spring-mass system x″ + 9x = 0 is released from x(0) = 0.1 m at rest. Find x at t = 1 s.

e^{−at} sin(ωt) ‖ ω/((s + a)^{2} + ω^{2}.title: Laplace pair: damped sine
e^{−at} sin(ωt) ‖ ω/((s + a)^{2} + ω^{2}.about: Complex poles at −a ± jω give an oscillation at ω inside an e^{−at} envelope: the underdamped response. Complete the square in the denominator to use it.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > −a

example.problem: Invert Y(s) = 1/(s^{2} + 2s + 5) and evaluate at t = 0.5.
steps: Complete the square: s^{2} + 2s + 5 = (s + 1)^{2} + 4, so a = 1, ω = 2

e^{−at} cos(ωt) ‖ (s + a)/((s + a)^{2} +.title: Laplace pair: damped cosine
e^{−at} cos(ωt) ‖ (s + a)/((s + a)^{2} +.about: The damped cosine has the same complex poles as the damped sine; its numerator is s + a. A general numerator splits into a multiple of (s + a) plus a multiple of ω.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > −a

example.problem: Invert Y(s) = (s + 3)/(s^{2} + 2s + 5) and evaluate at t = 0.5.

sinh(at) ‖ a/(s^{2} − a^{2}).title: Laplace pair: hyperbolic sine
sinh(at) ‖ a/(s^{2} − a^{2}).about: Real poles at ±a; sinh(at) = (e^{at} − e^{−at})/2. It shows up in unstable systems and beam or heat problems where the denominator is s^{2} − a^{2}.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > |a|

example.problem: Invert Y(s) = 4/(s^{2} − 4) and evaluate at t = 1.

cosh(at) ‖ s/(s^{2} − a^{2}).title: Laplace pair: hyperbolic cosine
cosh(at) ‖ s/(s^{2} − a^{2}).about: Real poles at ±a with a zero at the origin; cosh(at) = (e^{at} + e^{−at})/2.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > |a|

example.problem: Solve y″ − 9y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0, and find y(0.5).

f(t − a) u(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as} F(s).title: Laplace property: time shift (delay)
f(t − a) u(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as} F(s).about: Delaying a signal by a seconds multiplies its transform by e^{−as}. An e^{−as} factor in a transform means 'this part switches on at t = a'.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t); the u(t − a) matters: the shifted function is zero before t = a
a ≥ 0 (a delay, not an advance)
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0

example.problem: Invert e^{−2s}/(s + 1) and evaluate at t = 1 and t = 3.
steps: 1/(s + 1) ↔ e^{−t}, and e^{−2s} delays it by 2

e^{−at} f(t) ‖ F(s + a).title: Laplace property: frequency shift (exponential damping)
e^{−at} f(t) ‖ F(s + a).about: Multiplying by e^{−at} shifts the transform left by a: every pole moves from p to p − a. It turns the plain sine and cosine pairs into the damped ones.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
If F converges for Re(s) > σ_{0}, F(s + a) converges for Re(s) > σ_{0} − a
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0

example.problem: Invert (s + 2)/((s + 2)^{2} + 9) and evaluate at t = 0.5.

f(at), a > 0 ‖ (1/a) F(s/a).title: Laplace property: time scaling
f(at), a > 0 ‖ (1/a) F(s/a).about: Speeding a signal up by a factor a stretches its transform by a in s and scales it by 1/a. It follows by putting τ = at in the integral. A common mistake is writing F(as).
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
a > 0; a negative a would reverse time, which the one-sided transform can't represent
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0
related: f(t − a) u(t − a) ↔ e^{−as} F(s)

example.problem: From sin t ↔ 1/(s^{2} + 1), find the transform of sin(3t) and its value at s = 2.

df/dt ‖ s F(s) − f(0).title: Laplace property: derivative
df/dt ‖ s F(s) − f(0).about: Differentiation becomes multiplication by s, minus the initial value. This is what turns an initial-value problem into algebra, with the initial condition built in.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
f(0) is the value just before t = 0 (0⁻); with a jump at 0 that is the value before the jump
f must be of exponential order so its transform exists
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0

example.problem: Solve y′ + 3y = 0 with y(0) = 2, and find y(0.5).

d^{2}f/dt^{2} ‖ s^{2} F(s) − s f(0) − f′.title: Laplace property: second derivative
d^{2}f/dt^{2} ‖ s^{2} F(s) − s f(0) − f′.about: Two derivatives give s^{2}F(s) minus terms carrying the initial position and velocity. It solves second-order systems: springs, RLC circuits.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
f(0) and f′(0) are the values at 0⁻
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0

example.problem: Solve y″ + 5y′ + 6y = 0 with y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0, and find y(1).

∫_{0}^{t} f(τ) dτ ‖ F(s)/s.title: Laplace property: integral
∫_{0}^{t} f(τ) dτ ‖ F(s)/s.about: Integrating from 0 to t divides the transform by s. A factor 1/s in a transform means 'the running integral of the rest'.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
The integral starts at 0, so no initial-value term appears
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0

example.problem: Invert 1/(s(s^{2} + 1)) and evaluate at t = π.
steps: f = ∫_{0}^{t} sin τ dτ = 1 − cos t

t f(t) ‖ −dF/ds.title: Laplace property: multiplication by t
t f(t) ‖ −dF/ds.about: Multiplying by t differentiates the transform with respect to s (and flips its sign). It generates the repeated-pole pairs and handles resonance terms like t sin t.
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t)
Same region of convergence as F
vars: time function, taken as 0 for t < 0

example.problem: Find the transform of t sin t and its value at s = 1.

f(t) ∗ g(t) ‖ F(s) G(s).title: Laplace property: convolution
f(t) ∗ g(t) ‖ F(s) G(s).about: Convolution in time is multiplication in s. A system's output is its impulse response convolved with the input, so Y(s) = H(s)X(s).
assumptions: One-sided transform: only t ≥ 0 counts, so every pair stands for f(t) u(t); the convolution is (f ∗ g)(t) = ∫_{0}^{t} f(τ) g(t − τ) dτ
Valid where both transforms converge

example.problem: Find the inverse of 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) as e^{−t} ∗ e^{−2t}, and its value at t = 1.

f(0⁺) = lim_{s→∞} s F(s).title: Initial value theorem
f(0⁺) = lim_{s→∞} s F(s).about: As s → ∞, e^{−st} kills everything but the first instant, so s F(s) sees only f(0⁺). Read the starting value from the transform without inverting it; a quick check on a partial-fraction answer. A common mistake is using it on an improper F(s), which has an impulse at 0.
assumptions: F(s) must be strictly proper (numerator degree below denominator's); otherwise f has an impulse at 0 and the limit doesn't exist
Gives f(0⁺), which differs from f(0⁻) if f jumps at 0

steps: s F(s) = (2s^{2} + 3s)/(s^{2} + 3s + 2) → 2 as s → ∞ (ratio of leading coefficients)

f(∞) = lim_{s→0} s F(s).title: Final value theorem
f(∞) = lim_{s→0} s F(s).about: The steady-state value of f can be read from the transform near s = 0. It gives steady-state error and DC gain in control. A common mistake is applying it when f doesn't settle (a pole in the right half-plane or on the jω axis other than s = 0).
assumptions: Only if f settles: every pole of sF(s) is in the open left half-plane
It gives wrong answers otherwise: for F = 1/(s^{2} + 1) (sin t) it returns 0, though sin t never settles
related: DC gain of a stable system

example.problem: A step response has Y(s) = 10/(s(s + 5)). What value does y settle to?
steps: sY = 10/(s + 5), with its only pole at −5 (stable)

X(z) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n] z^{−n}.title: z transform (two-sided definition)
X(z) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n] z^{−n}.about: The z transform turns a sequence into a function of the complex variable z; each z^{−1} is a delay of one sample. It is the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform, used to analyse digital filters and difference equations.
assumptions: The sum converges only in an annulus r_{1} < |z| < r_{2}, the region of convergence (ROC); a transform is incomplete without it
Right-sided sequences have ROCs outside a circle, left-sided inside one, two-sided in a ring
A system is stable when its ROC includes the unit circle |z| = 1; there X(e^{jω}) is the DTFT
related: link to the Laplace variable, sample period T

example.problem: Find X(z) for x = {1, 2, 3} at n = 0, 1, 2 (zero elsewhere), and evaluate it at z = 2.

u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − z^{−1}).title: z-transform pair: unit step
u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − z^{−1}).about: The discrete step is 1 for n ≥ 0. Its transform has a pole at z = 1, which is also the transfer function of an accumulator y[n] = y[n − 1] + x[n].
assumptions: ROC |z| > 1: the geometric series Σ z^{−n} converges only there
The pole sits on the unit circle, so the accumulator is marginally stable

example.problem: Check the pair at z = 2, inside the ROC, by summing the series.
steps: At z = 1/2, outside the ROC, the terms 2^{n} grow and the sum diverges

a^{n} u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − az^{−1}).title: z-transform pair: causal exponential
a^{n} u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − az^{−1}).about: A right-sided geometric sequence has a single pole at z = a. It is the impulse response of the first-order recursive filter y[n] = a y[n − 1] + x[n].
assumptions: ROC |z| > |a|, outside the pole
Stable (ROC includes |z| = 1) only if |a| < 1
The same formula with ROC |z| < |a| is the left-sided −a^{n} u[−n − 1]

example.problem: The filter y[n] = 0.5 y[n − 1] + x[n] has h[n] = 0.5^{n} u[n]. Find its DC gain H(1).

−a^{n} u[−n − 1] ‖ 1/(1 − az^{−1}).title: z-transform pair: anticausal exponential
−a^{n} u[−n − 1] ‖ 1/(1 − az^{−1}).about: A left-sided sequence (nonzero only for n ≤ −1) has the same formula as a^{n}u[n] but the opposite ROC. It is why a z transform must state its ROC to be inverted uniquely.
assumptions: ROC |z| < |a|, inside the pole
Stable (ROC includes |z| = 1) only if |a| > 1
Anticausal: a real-time system can't produce it, but offline processing can

example.problem: X(z) = 1/(1 − 2z^{−1}) with ROC |z| < 2 (which contains the unit circle). Find x[n] and check X(1).
steps: ROC inside the pole: x[n] = −2^{n} u[−n − 1] = −1/2, −1/4, … at n = −1, −2, …

n a^{n} u[n] ‖ az^{−1}/(1 − az^{−1})^{2}.title: z-transform pair: n times an exponential (double pole)
n a^{n} u[n] ‖ az^{−1}/(1 − az^{−1})^{2}.about: A double pole at z = a gives n a^{n}, the discrete version of t e^{−at}. It follows from the n x[n] ↔ −z dX/dz property.
assumptions: ROC |z| > |a|
Stable if |a| < 1

example.problem: With a = 0.5, evaluate the transform at z = 1 and check it by summing the sequence.

cos(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ (1 − cos(ω_{o}) z^{−1.title: z-transform pair: causal cosine
cos(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ (1 − cos(ω_{o}) z^{−1.about: A cosine switched on at n = 0 has poles on the unit circle at e^{±jω_{o}}. Its denominator gives a two-pole digital oscillator.
assumptions: ROC |z| > 1
Poles on the unit circle: marginally stable, a sustained oscillation
ω_{o} in radians per sample (0 to π)

example.problem: With ω_{o} = π/3, write the difference equation the pair implies and run it from an impulse for four samples.

sin(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ sin(ω_{o}) z^{−1}/(1.title: z-transform pair: causal sine
sin(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ sin(ω_{o}) z^{−1}/(1.about: A sine switched on at n = 0 has the same unit-circle poles as the cosine, with a numerator sin(ω_{o})z^{−1}. Driving that system with an impulse generates a sampled sine wave.
assumptions: ROC |z| > 1
Poles on the unit circle: marginally stable
ω_{o} in radians per sample

example.problem: With ω_{o} = π/2, find the oscillator's difference equation and its output for n = 0 … 4.
steps: From an impulse: 0, 1, 0, −1, 0 = sin(πn/2); y[3] = sin(3π/2) = −1

x[n − n_{o}] ‖ z^{−n_{o}} X(z).title: z-transform property: time shift
x[n − n_{o}] ‖ z^{−n_{o}} X(z).about: Delaying a sequence by n_{o} samples multiplies its transform by z^{−n_{o}}. This is why z^{−1} is drawn as a one-sample delay block in filter diagrams.
assumptions: Two-sided transform; the ROC is unchanged except possibly at z = 0 or ∞
For the one-sided transform, a delay also brings in initial-condition terms
vars: delay in samples (negative for an advance)
related: transfer function of a difference equation

example.problem: An echo filter y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n − 3]. Find H(z) and the gain at ω = π/3, where z^{−3} = e^{−jπ} = −1.

a^{n} x[n] ‖ X(z/a).title: z-transform property: multiplication by a^{n} (scaling in z)
a^{n} x[n] ‖ X(z/a).about: Multiplying a sequence by a^{n} scales the z-plane: every pole and zero moves from p to a p. It turns the step into a geometric sequence and a cosine into a damped one.
assumptions: If X converges for r_{1} < |z| < r_{2}, the result converges for |a| r_{1} < |z| < |a| r_{2}

example.problem: From u[n] ↔ 1/(1 − z^{−1}), find the transform of 0.8^{n} u[n] and its value at z = 1.

n x[n] ‖ −z dX/dz.title: z-transform property: multiplication by n
n x[n] ‖ −z dX/dz.about: Multiplying a sequence by n corresponds to differentiating its transform and multiplying by −z. It produces the repeated-pole pairs.
assumptions: Same ROC as X(z), except possibly z = 0 or ∞

example.problem: From a^{n}u[n] ↔ z/(z − a), find the transform of n a^{n} u[n] and check it at a = 0.5, z = 2.

x[−n] ‖ X(1/z).title: z-transform property: time reversal
x[−n] ‖ X(1/z).about: Flipping a sequence in time replaces z by 1/z: poles move to their reciprocals and the ROC turns inside out.
assumptions: If X converges for r_{1} < |z| < r_{2}, X(1/z) converges for 1/r_{2} < |z| < 1/r_{1}
A causal sequence becomes anticausal

example.problem: Reverse x[n] = 0.5^{n} u[n]. Find the transform, its ROC, and its value at z = 1.

x[n] ∗ h[n] ‖ X(z) H(z).title: z-transform property: convolution
x[n] ∗ h[n] ‖ X(z) H(z).about: Convolving two sequences multiplies their transforms. A digital filter's output is Y(z) = H(z)X(z), and multiplying polynomials in z^{−1} is convolving their coefficients. A common mistake is forgetting the ROC: it is at least the overlap of the two.
assumptions: ROC contains at least the intersection of the two ROCs (larger if poles cancel)
Convolution: y[n] = Σ_{k} x[k] h[n − k]

example.problem: Convolve x = {1, 1} with h = {1, 2, 1} using z transforms.

δ(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as}.title: Laplace pair: delayed impulse
δ(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as}.about: An impulse at t = a transforms to the pure delay factor e^{−as}. It models a sudden kick or hammer blow at a known time.
assumptions: a ≥ 0: an impulse before t = 0 lies outside the one-sided transform
ROC: every s
related: f(t − a) u(t − a) ↔ e^{−as} F(s)

example.problem: Find the transform of 5δ(t − 2).

u(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as}/s.title: Laplace pair: delayed unit step (Heaviside)
u(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as}/s.about: A step switched on at t = a. Use it to write piecewise inputs: a pulse from a to b is u(t − a) − u(t − b). A common mistake is writing f(t) u(t − a) and transforming it as e^{−as}F(s); the function must be shifted too, f(t − a)u(t − a).
assumptions: ROC Re(s) > 0
related: f(t − a) u(t − a) ↔ e^{−as} F(s)

example.problem: Transform a pulse of height 3 from t = 1 to t = 4.

1 − e^{−at} ‖ a/(s(s + a)).title: Laplace pair: first-order rise to 1
1 − e^{−at} ‖ a/(s(s + a)).about: The step response of a first-order system with time constant 1/a, such as an RC circuit charging. A common mistake is dropping the a on top: 1/(s(s + a)) is (1 − e^{−at})/a.
assumptions: a > 0, so the response settles at 1
ROC Re(s) > 0

example.problem: Invert 5/(s(s + 5)) and evaluate at t = 0.2 s (one time constant).

(e^{−at} − e^{−bt})/(b − a) ‖ 1/((s + a).title: Laplace pair: two distinct real poles
(e^{−at} − e^{−bt})/(b − a) ‖ 1/((s + a).about: Partial fractions give 1/((s + a)(s + b)) = (1/(b − a))(1/(s + a) − 1/(s + b)), and each term is an exponential. It inverts two first-order factors in one step. A common mistake is the order: (b − a) goes with e^{−at} − e^{−bt}; swapping one flips the sign.
assumptions: a ≠ b; for a = b use t e^{−at}
ROC Re(s) > max(−a, −b)
vars: pole locations, −a and −b, with a ≠ b

example.problem: Invert 1/((s + 1)(s + 3)) and evaluate at t = 1 s.

t sin(ωt) ‖ 2ωs/(s^{2} + ω^{2})^{2}.title: Laplace pair: t times a sine
t sin(ωt) ‖ 2ωs/(s^{2} + ω^{2})^{2}.about: A sine whose envelope grows linearly: the response of an undamped oscillator driven at resonance. Comes from −d/ds of the sine pair.
assumptions: One-sided: stands for t sin(ωt) u(t)
ROC Re(s) > 0

example.problem: Invert s/(s^{2} + 4)^{2} and evaluate at t = 1 s.

t cos(ωt) ‖ (s^{2} − ω^{2})/(s^{2} + ω^{.title: Laplace pair: t times a cosine
t cos(ωt) ‖ (s^{2} − ω^{2})/(s^{2} + ω^{.about: Comes from the multiply-by-t rule: −d/ds of s/(s^{2} + ω^{2}). A double pole pair on the jω axis, so it shows up when an undamped system is driven at its own resonance.
assumptions: One-sided: stands for t cos(ωt) u(t)
Region of convergence Re(s) > 0

example.problem: Transform t cos(3t) and evaluate it at s = 1.

a f(t) + b g(t) ‖ a F(s) + b G(s).title: Laplace property: linearity
a f(t) + b g(t) ‖ a F(s) + b G(s).about: The defining integral is linear, so the transform of a weighted sum is the weighted sum of the transforms; transform term by term with the table. A common mistake is transforming a product as a product: the transform of f g is not F G (F G is the transform of the convolution).
assumptions: Both transforms exist; the ROC is at least the overlap of theirs

example.problem: Transform 3 + 2e^{−t}, and evaluate it at s = 1.

d^{n}f/dt^{n} ‖ s^{n} F(s) − Σ_{k=1}^{n}.title: Laplace property: nth derivative
d^{n}f/dt^{n} ‖ s^{n} F(s) − Σ_{k=1}^{n}.about: Integrating by parts n times trades each derivative for a factor s and drops an initial value, which is how an ODE becomes algebra. A common mistake is pairing the powers wrongly: s^{n−1} goes with f(0), and s^{0} with f^{(n−1)}(0).
assumptions: f and its first n − 1 derivatives are known at 0⁻
f is of exponential order

example.problem: Transform y′′′ with y(0) = 1 and y′(0) = y′′(0) = 0.

z = e^{jω}.title: The unit circle in the z-plane is the DTFT
z = e^{jω}.about: On |z| = 1 the z transform becomes the DTFT: X(e^{jω}) = X(z) at z = e^{jω}. So the DTFT exists when the ROC includes the unit circle.
assumptions: Valid only if the ROC of X(z) includes the unit circle |z| = 1
ω = 0 is z = 1 (DC); ω = π is z = −1 (the highest frequency)

example.problem: Get the DTFT of a^{n}u[n] (|a| < 1) from its z transform.

z = e^{sT}.title: Mapping the s-plane to the z-plane
z = e^{sT}.about: Sampling every T seconds maps a pole at s to one at z = e^{sT}. The left half-plane goes inside the unit circle, so stable stays stable. A common mistake is mapping with z = 1 + sT; that is only Euler's first-order approximation.
assumptions: The jω axis maps onto |z| = 1 and the left half-plane inside it
s and s + j2π/T map to the same z: that is aliasing
related: the unit circle is the DTFT

example.problem: A pole at s = −10 is sampled at T = 0.01 s. Where is it in z?

δ[n − m] ‖ z^{−m}.title: z-transform pair: delayed unit sample
δ[n − m] ‖ z^{−m}.about: A sample at n = m is m delays: z^{−m}. Every FIR filter is a sum of these. A common mistake is z^{+m} for a delay; delays carry negative powers.
assumptions: m an integer
ROC every z except 0 for m > 0, except ∞ for m < 0

example.problem: Transform h[n] = δ[n] + 2δ[n − 1] + δ[n − 2], and find its DC gain H(1).

n u[n] ‖ z^{−1}/(1 − z^{−1})^{2}.title: z-transform pair: unit ramp
n u[n] ‖ z^{−1}/(1 − z^{−1})^{2}.about: The sampled ramp 0, 1, 2, …: apply n x[n] ↔ −z dX/dz to u[n] ↔ 1/(1 − z^{−1}). It has a double pole at z = 1, as t ↔ 1/s^{2} has a double pole at s = 0. A common mistake is 1/(1 − z^{−1})^{2}, which is (n + 1)u[n].
assumptions: ROC |z| > 1
The double pole on the unit circle makes it unbounded, as the ramp is

example.problem: Write the ramp transform with positive powers of z, and check it at z = 2.
steps: multiply top and bottom by z^{2}: z/(z − 1)^{2}

r^{n} cos(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ (1 − r cos(ω_{o.title: z-transform pair: damped cosine
r^{n} cos(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ (1 − r cos(ω_{o.about: A cosine decaying by r each sample; its poles are at z = re^{±jω_{o}}. The response of a resonant digital filter. A common mistake is putting the poles at r and ω_{o} in rectangular form; they are re^{±jω_{o}}.
assumptions: ROC |z| > r
Stable when r < 1; r = 1 is the undamped cosine

example.problem: Where are the poles for r = 0.9, ω_{o} = π/4?

r^{n} sin(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ r sin(ω_{o}) z^.title: z-transform pair: damped sine
r^{n} sin(ω_{o}n) u[n] ‖ r sin(ω_{o}) z^.about: Write sin(ω_{o}n) as (e^{jω_{o}n} − e^{−jω_{o}n})/(2j): two geometric sequences (re^{±jω_{o}})^{n} with poles at z = re^{±jω_{o}}. Same poles as the damped cosine; only the numerator differs. A common mistake is r^{2} in the numerator; it is r once.
assumptions: ROC |z| > r
Stable when r < 1; r = 1 is the undamped sine

example.problem: Find X(z) for r = 0.5, ω_{o} = π/2, and x[3].

a x[n] + b y[n] ‖ a X(z) + b Y(z).title: z-transform property: linearity
a x[n] + b y[n] ‖ a X(z) + b Y(z).about: The defining sum is linear, so the transform of a weighted sum is the weighted sum of the transforms; the ROC is at least the overlap of the two. A common mistake is assuming the ROC can't grow: a pole can cancel and widen it.
assumptions: ROC at least the intersection of the two ROCs
related: what a product of transforms is

example.problem: Transform 2u[n] − δ[n], and evaluate it at z = 2.

x[n] − x[n − 1] ‖ (1 − z^{−1}) X(z).title: z-transform property: first difference
x[n] − x[n − 1] ‖ (1 − z^{−1}) X(z).about: The delayed copy transforms to z^{−1}X(z), so the difference is (1 − z^{−1})X(z): a zero at z = 1 that blocks DC, the discrete derivative. A common mistake is writing (z − 1)X(z); that is one sample ahead.
assumptions: ROC at least that of X(z), except possibly z = 0

example.problem: Find the first difference of u[n] from transforms.

Σ_{k=−∞}^{n} x[k] ‖ X(z)/(1 − z^{−1}).title: z-transform property: accumulation
Σ_{k=−∞}^{n} x[k] ‖ X(z)/(1 − z^{−1}).about: A running sum is x convolved with u[n], whose transform is 1/(1 − z^{−1}); so accumulating divides by (1 − z^{−1}), a pole at z = 1: the discrete integrator. A common mistake is keeping X's ROC; the new one must also exclude |z| ≤ 1.
assumptions: ROC at least the overlap of X's ROC with |z| > 1

example.problem: Find the transform of the running sum of 0.5^{n}u[n], and where it settles.
steps: Final value: (z − 1) times it at z → 1 = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2

x[0] = lim_{z→∞} X(z).title: Initial value theorem (z transform)
x[0] = lim_{z→∞} X(z).about: For a causal sequence, letting z grow kills every z^{−n} term but the first, leaving x[0]. A common mistake is multiplying by (z − 1) as in the final value theorem; here it is X(z) alone.
assumptions: x[n] = 0 for n < 0

x[∞] = lim_{z→1} (z − 1) X(z).title: Final value theorem (z transform)
x[∞] = lim_{z→1} (z − 1) X(z).about: Gives where a causal sequence settles, without inverting. Only valid if it settles: every pole of (z − 1)X(z) inside the unit circle. A common mistake is using it on an oscillating or growing x; the number it returns then means nothing.
assumptions: x[n] causal
poles of (z − 1)X(z) inside |z| = 1

example.problem: A system with H(z) = 0.2/(1 − 0.8z^{−1}) gets a unit step. Where does the output settle?

f(t) = (1/2πj) ∫_{σ−j∞}^{σ+j∞} F(s) e^{s.title: Inverse Laplace transform (Bromwich integral)
f(t) = (1/2πj) ∫_{σ−j∞}^{σ+j∞} F(s) e^{s.about: Recovers f(t) from F(s) by integrating up a vertical line in the s-plane to the right of every pole. In practice you rarely evaluate it: split F(s) into partial fractions and read each term off the table.
assumptions: σ lies in the region of convergence, to the right of every pole of F(s)
Gives f(t) for t > 0 (the one-sided transform says nothing about t < 0)
vars: real part of the integration line
related: f(t) = Σ residues of F(s) e^{st}
closing the contour: one term per pole

example.problem: Invert F(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) and evaluate f(1).

F(s) = A_{1}/(s − p_{1}) + A_{2}/(s − p_.title: Partial fractions for an inverse Laplace transform
F(s) = A_{1}/(s − p_{1}) + A_{2}/(s − p_.about: Write a proper rational F(s) as a sum of simple terms, one per pole, then invert each from the table: A/(s − p) ↔ A e^{pt}. This is the standard route for an inverse Laplace transform and for solving an ODE.
assumptions: F proper (numerator degree below denominator); divide first if not
Distinct poles here; repeated and complex poles have their own rows

example.problem: Find f(t) for F(s) = (s + 3)/((s + 1)(s + 2)), and f(1).

A_{i} = [(s − p_{i}) F(s)]_{s = p_{i}}.title: Cover-up rule (residue at a simple pole)
A_{i} = [(s − p_{i}) F(s)]_{s = p_{i}}.about: To find the coefficient of 1/(s − p_{i}), cancel that factor from the denominator and set s = p_{i} in what is left. It works for complex poles too, giving complex-conjugate residues.
assumptions: p_{i} a simple (unrepeated) pole
F proper

example.problem: F(s) = 10/(s(s + 5)). Find the residues and f(t).

A_{r−k} = (1/k!) [d^{k}/ds^{k} ((s − p)^.title: Partial fractions with a repeated pole
A_{r−k} = (1/k!) [d^{k}/ds^{k} ((s − p)^.about: A pole p of order r needs r terms A_{1}/(s − p) + … + A_{r}/(s − p)^{r}. Multiply by (s − p)^{r}; the value at s = p gives A_{r}, and each further derivative (over k!) gives the next one down. A_{j}/(s − p)^{j} inverts to A_{j} t^{j−1} e^{pt}/(j − 1)!.
assumptions: F proper

s^{2} + bs + c = (s + b/2)^{2} + (c − b^.title: Completing the square for complex poles
s^{2} + bs + c = (s + b/2)^{2} + (c − b^.about: When s^{2} + bs + c has complex roots (b^{2} < 4c), write it as (s + a)^{2} + ω^{2} with a = b/2 and ω = √(c − b^{2}/4). Then split the numerator into (s + a) and a constant and use the damped cosine and sine pairs.
assumptions: b^{2} < 4c; otherwise factor into real poles

example.problem: Invert F(s) = (s + 3)/(s^{2} + 2s + 5) and evaluate at t = π/4.
steps: s + 3 = (s + 1) + 2, so f = e^{−t} cos 2t + e^{−t} sin 2t

H(s) = Y(s)/X(s).title: Transfer function
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s).about: The ratio of the output transform to the input transform with every initial condition zero. Its poles give the natural response; the system is stable when all poles have negative real part. Y(s) = H(s)X(s), and h(t) is the inverse transform of H.
assumptions: LTI system, zero initial conditions
Stable: every pole in the left half-plane

example.problem: An RC low-pass has RC dy/dt + y = x with R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 µF. Find H(s) and its pole.
steps: RC sY + Y = X, so H = 1/(RC s + 1)

F(s) = (1/(1 − e^{−sT})) ∫_{0}^{T} f(t).title: Laplace transform of a periodic function
F(s) = (1/(1 − e^{−sT})) ∫_{0}^{T} f(t).about: For f repeating every T, transform one period and divide by 1 − e^{−sT}; the factor sums the geometric series of delayed copies. Used for square-wave or sawtooth inputs in ODE problems.
assumptions: f(t + T) = f(t) for t ≥ 0
related: f(t − a) u(t − a) ↔ e^{−as} F(s)

example.problem: f = 1 for 0 < t < 1, 0 for 1 < t < 2, repeating (T = 2). Find F(1).

g(t) u(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as} ℒ{g(t + a.title: Laplace of a function switched on at t = a
g(t) u(t − a), a ≥ 0 ‖ e^{−as} ℒ{g(t + a.about: For a piecewise function, write each piece as g(t) u(t − a). The shift theorem needs the function written in t − a; this form skips that: transform g(t + a) and multiply by e^{−as}.
related: f(t − a) u(t − a) ↔ e^{−as} F(s)

example.problem: Find ℒ{t u(t − 2)} and its value at s = 1.

u[n] − u[n − N] ‖ (1 − z^{−N})/(1 − z^{−.title: Z pair: length-N rectangular window
u[n] − u[n − N] ‖ (1 − z^{−N})/(1 − z^{−.about: N ones starting at n = 0. The sum 1 + z^{−1} + … + z^{−(N−1)} is a finite geometric series, so the ROC is every z but 0. Its zeros are the N-th roots of unity except z = 1: it is the moving-average (boxcar) FIR filter, times N.
assumptions: ROC all z ≠ 0 (finite length)
related: the step it is built from

example.problem: Evaluate the length-4 window's X(z) at z = 2.

|z| > max|p_{i}|.title: Right-sided (causal) sequence: region of convergence
|z| > max|p_{i}|.about: A right-sided sequence converges outside a circle through its largest pole: the ROC is everything beyond the outermost pole, out to ∞. The same X(z) can belong to several sequences; the ROC picks which, so always state it.
assumptions: x[n] = 0 for n < some N₀
The ROC never contains a pole

example.problem: X(z) = 1/((1 − 0.5z^{−1})(1 − 2z^{−1})) and x is causal. Find the ROC; is x stable?
steps: Poles at 0.5 and 2: outside the outer one

|z| < min|p_{i}|.title: Left-sided sequence: region of convergence
|z| < min|p_{i}|.about: A left-sided (anti-causal) sequence converges inside a circle through its smallest pole. Each term A/(1 − pz^{−1}) then inverts to −A p^{n} u[−n − 1].
assumptions: x[n] = 0 for n > some N₁

example.problem: X(z) = 1/((1 − 0.5z^{−1})(1 − 2z^{−1})) is left-sided. Find the ROC.

r_{1} < |z| < r_{2}.title: Two-sided sequence: region of convergence
r_{1} < |z| < r_{2}.about: A two-sided sequence converges in a ring between two adjacent poles. Poles inside the ring give right-sided terms (p^{n} u[n]); poles outside give left-sided terms (−p^{n} u[−n − 1]). With N distinct pole radii there are N + 1 possible ROCs.
assumptions: Bounded by poles; contains none

|p_{i}| < 1 for every pole.title: Stability of a causal system from its poles
|p_{i}| < 1 for every pole.about: An LTI system is stable when its ROC contains the unit circle. For a causal system (ROC outside the outermost pole) that means every pole of H(z) lies strictly inside the unit circle.
assumptions: Causal system; poles of H(z) after cancelling common factors
related: left half-plane maps inside the unit circle

example.problem: H(z) has denominator z^{2} − z + 0.5. Is the causal system stable?

X(z) = Σ A_{i}/(1 − p_{i} z^{−1}).title: Inverse z transform by partial fractions
X(z) = Σ A_{i}/(1 − p_{i} z^{−1}).about: Expand X(z) in powers of z^{−1}, one term per pole, then invert each with the ROC: right-sided gives A_{i} p_{i}^{n} u[n]. (Or expand X(z)/z in z and multiply back by z; both give the same answer.)
assumptions: Distinct poles; numerator degree in z^{−1} below the denominator's (else divide first)
ROC |z| > max|p_{i}| for the causal answer

A_{i} = [(1 − p_{i} z^{−1}) X(z)]_{z = p.title: Cover-up rule for the z transform
A_{i} = [(1 − p_{i} z^{−1}) X(z)]_{z = p.about: Cancel the factor (1 − p_{i} z^{−1}) and set z = p_{i} in the rest. Note that z^{−1} becomes 1/p_{i}, a common slip.
assumptions: p_{i} a simple pole

H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) = (Σ b_{k} z^{−k})/(Σ a.title: Transfer function from a difference equation
H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) = (Σ b_{k} z^{−k})/(Σ a.about: Each delay y[n − k] becomes z^{−k}Y(z), so a linear difference equation gives H(z) as a ratio of polynomials in z^{−1}. Its poles decide stability; on the unit circle it is the frequency response; H(1) is the DC gain.
assumptions: LTI, zero initial conditions
a₀ = 1 by convention
related: Response ‖ H(e^{jω}) = (Σ b_{k} e^{−jωk})/(Σ a_{k} e^{−jωk})

example.problem: y[n] − 0.5y[n − 1] = x[n] + x[n − 1]. Find H(z) and its DC gain.

x[n − 1] ‖ z^{−1} X(z) + x[−1].title: One-sided z transform of a delay
x[n − 1] ‖ z^{−1} X(z) + x[−1].about: The unilateral transform starts at n = 0, so delaying by one brings in the initial condition x[−1]. Use it to solve a difference equation with given initial values (the z analogue of sF(s) − f(0)).
assumptions: One-sided transform X(z) = Σ_{n=0}^{∞} x[n] z^{−n}
Two delays: z^{−2}X + z^{−1}x[−1] + x[−2]

example.problem: y[n] − 0.5y[n − 1] = 0 with y[−1] = 2. Find y[n] and y[3].
